title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Wixom passes noise and cost limits as AG Nessel fights secret DTE deals.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Monday morning, August 17, and we're diving into fresh local action on data centers plus a big transparency fight from the attorney general.
Yeah, yesterday's vote in Wixom really caught my eye. A 4-3 decision to back new zoning rules limiting noise and utility costs for a huge proposed project.
Exactly. That 600,000-square-foot facility on 54 acres is on hold during a 180-day moratorium, and residents have been vocal about power demand, water use, and noise that could hit household bills.
So what does this actually change on the ground? How does a local zoning tweak affect something as big as electric rates?

It sets stricter standards the developer has to meet before any approvals move forward. The rules target noise levels and try to cap how much extra power and water infrastructure the project can demand from the city.
I've been wondering about the bigger picture here. Michigan towns have been wrestling with these proposals for a while now — what's the history that led to this kind of pushback?

It's been building across southern Michigan. Utilities and developers have been scouting sites, and communities started realizing these facilities pull massive amounts of electricity and water while generating steady noise. Towns like Wixom are using moratoriums and new ordinances to buy time and set guardrails.
And the stakes feel real for everyday folks. Higher utility bills, strain on water supplies, and changes to the character of farmland or small towns — how directly does one project ripple out?

One large data center can add significant load to the grid, which utilities sometimes pass along through rate adjustments. Water use for cooling is another concern in areas already managing resources. Noise carries, and industrial zoning can shift property values or daily life for neighbors.
What happens next in Wixom? Does the 4-3 vote lock this in, or is there more debate coming?

The changes advance during the moratorium, so the council will keep refining them. Developers will likely respond with revised plans, and residents will have more chances to weigh in at future meetings.
It feels like a template other places might copy. How much precedent could this set?

Quite a bit. Wixom's approach shows towns can push back on specific impacts without outright banning the projects. Nearby communities watching power and water concerns will probably look at similar language.
Shifting to the other big development from the weekend — Attorney General Nessel asking the Court of Appeals to reopen a hearing on those secret DTE contracts for the Saline project.
Right. She's arguing that ratepayers deserve to see the terms and costs. The case could force more openness on how these deals get negotiated across the state.
Why keep contracts hidden in the first place? What are people worried about if the details stay private?

The concern is that hidden terms could mean ratepayers end up subsidizing big infrastructure upgrades without knowing the full picture. Lost tax revenue for local governments is another angle if incentives aren't public.
And this isn't the first time we've seen pushback on transparency with these projects, is it?
No, it's part of a pattern. Communities keep asking for clearer information on who benefits and who pays when these hyperscale facilities come online.
What could the appeals court decision mean for future projects?
If Nessel wins, it might require more public review of utility agreements statewide. That could slow some deals but give towns better leverage on costs and impacts.
Okay, let's hit the quick hits. Marshall dropping charges tied to data center threats — what's the latest there?
Calhoun County officials said today no one will face charges over threats made during debates on a proposed center. The city council is still weighing tax breaks and power upgrades.
Residents there are worried about bills and noise too. Moving on, Branch County cities meeting today to hash out rules — how far could those changes reach?

Two local governments in Branch County are holding a joint session on data center proposals. Any new power and noise rules could affect residents up to 30 miles away if sites connect to the same grid.
Mason City Council resumes debate tonight on a nearby hyperscale proposal and noise ordinance.
Yes, they'll revisit zoning and the citizen-initiated noise rules tied to the Vevay Township project. Jackson County is also looking at personal property tax rules.
And Cass County residents packed a hall over the weekend to push back on projects.
Save Cass County drew a standing-room crowd voicing worries over noise, water, and electric bills. They're urging officials to reject or restrict proposals before more land gets optioned.
Saline Township hired a retired sergeant to handle zoning fights — smart move with more projects likely coming?
It signals they're preparing for complex cases. Residents near Ann Arbor now have a dedicated contact for big industrial proposals including potential data centers.
Now for on deck — what meetings can listeners actually attend today?
Several. Mason City Council revisits the data center zoning and noise rules for the Vevay Township proposal.
Coldwater has a joint session with the Planning Commission and Board of Public Utilities — MSU Extension is presenting on impacts and possible local ordinances.
Caledonia Township Planning Commission is discussing a data center ordinance covering high-intensity uses, electrical and water demands, and possibly extending a moratorium.
Kalamazoo City Commission votes on a temporary moratorium resolution.
And the City of Coldwater Planning Commission and CBPU Board meet again on zoning for high-utility data centers.
Plenty for folks to check out if they're near any of those spots.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Wixom Zoning Win and AG's Push for Contract Transparency
